title: VPC golden paths and fallback guidance (on-prem & airgapped) - draft
content:
Purpose:
This is an engineer-facing draft that codifies the "golden paths" we recommend for customer VPC and on-prem network onboarding, plus pragmatic fallback guidance for non-ideal environments (legacy firewalls, limited routing, strict egress controls, and airgapped sites). The goal is to shrink onboarding time by surfacing standard topologies, Terraform module interfaces we expect to be stable, and the pragmatic upgrade/rollback steps we follow when a tenant is mid-migration.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: Solutions engineers, platform engineers, SREs doing customer onboarding for Private deployments (VPC, on-prem connectors, and airgapped bundles).
- Scope: Reference topologies (3 golden paths), Terraform module guidance (interface and compatibility notes), a phased upgrade plan for tenant network changes, and a compact runbook for last-resort fallbacks.

High-level assumptions (do sanity checks before starting):
- Customer can create at least one dedicated subnet and a pair of route tables.
- We have an agreed CIDR range (no overlap with Redwood-managed subnets).
- Customer security team accepts outbound TLS (443) to our control-plane endpoints OR a connectivity tunnel for airgapped installs.
- Owner has SSH/console access or a vendor contact for on-prem firewall changes.

Golden path #1 — Cloud-native transit (recommended default)
Topology summary: customer VPC -> Transit Gateway / Cloud Router -> Redwood private endpoints in customer VPC (service endpoints or internal ALBs).
Why: minimizes NAT/egress complexity, allows central inspection, simple routing.
Key infra pieces to request from customer:
- VPC with two AZ subnets for HA, route propagation enabled on the transit gateway, peering attachment created.
- Security group rules: outbound 443 to our control-plane and 8443 for runtime if using direct control-plane.
Terraform notes (module interface):
- module.redwood-private-vpc expects: customer_cidr (string), public_subnets (list), private_subnets (list), transit_attachment_id (string|null).
- Output contracts: redwood_ingress_cidrs (list), client_vpn_endpoint (string|null).
Compatibility: works when TGW supports route propagation. If customer uses cloud vendor-specific firewall appliances in-line, escalate to network team.

Golden path #2 — Direct cross-connect (low-latency/high-control)
Topology summary: Dedicated cross-connect or Direct Connect equivalent into colo -> internal load balancer -> Redwood runtime cluster.
Why: necessary for ultra-low-latency or regulated workloads where traffic must never traverse public interconnects.
Key asks: VLAN/QoS details, BGP peer addresses, MTU requirements, and an on-site network engineer.
Terraform notes: treat the connection as a data source (we do not provision DX itself); module arguments include bgp_asn (number), peer_cidrs (list), bgp_password (sensitive string).
Testing: once provisioned, validate BGP session state and run 1-minute pings from representative host to runtime LB.

Golden path #3 — Airgapped / limited egress (special-case)
Topology summary: On-prem cluster (airgapped) with a one-way package sync VM / pull-mirror and a control-plane proxy run by customer in their network.
Why: regulatory or extremely strict security requirements.
Pattern limitations: no remote debug, no telemetry by default; update cadence is slower.
Installer notes: Provide a signed bundle (tar.gz) and a small bootstrap VM image with config. We'll require a documented maintenance window for package sync.

Terraform module compatibility and upgrade rules
- Semantic versioning policy: Major bumps are breaking (change required), minor bumps are additive, patches are bugfixes.
- Module interface stability: keep variables stable for common fields (cidr, subnets, firewall_rules). Add new optional vars instead of reshaping interfaces.
- Migration pattern for breaking module change:
  1) Create new module major version branch (eg v2/) and a migration helper script that maps v1 state to v2 variables.
  2) Deploy v2 in a canary tenant (non-prod) and validate with full acceptance tests.
  3) Offer customer a maintenance window for migration — apply terraform plan in drift-detection mode first, review diff with customer network owner.
  4) Roll forward only after post-plan validation.
Rollback guidance: keep last-applied terraform state archived with a timestamp and provider versioning. To rollback, restore archived state in a dry-run environment and run terraform apply against the restored state.

Upgrade plan — phased network cutover (recommended minimal disruption)
Phase A — Discovery (1–3 days):
- Inventory routes, firewall rules, NATs, load-balancers, overlapping CIDR conflicts.
- Confirm maintenance windows and the customer contact list.
Phase B — Prep & shadow (2–5 days):
- Create shadow route tables and mirror security rules to new subnets.
- Create temporary peering/TGW attachments without propagating routes to production route tables.
Phase C — Canary cut (2–4 hours in window):
- Move one service/ALB target group to the new subnet via weighted DNS or LB target swap.
- Execute smoke tests (see below).
Phase D — Full cutover (2–8 hours):
- Propagate routes to production tables, remove legacy NATs if desired, and monitor for errors for 2x SLA window.
Phase E — Cleanup (1–3 days):
- Remove shadow artifacts and archive terraform plans/state.

Smoke tests and validation checklist (run during and after cut):
- Control-plane checks: curl -fsS https://<control-plane-endpoint>/healthz (200 expected).
- Runtime checks: simple GPT-completion request through the runtime endpoint and validate latency < expected 2x baseline.
- Connectivity: traceroute to runtime LB from two AZs, verify expected AS path.
- e2e: run 50 synthetic requests over 10 minutes, assert success rate > 99% and token latency.
- Observability: ensure that token-cost breakdowns appear in Redwood Console within 15 minutes.

Fallback tactics (when golden path fails)
- If TGW or peering is blocked: use a bastion-host based reverse-proxy pattern. Deploy a small reverse-proxy VM in customer VPC that tunnels to a Redwood-managed proxy in a public subnet; lock it down to only required ports.
- If egress 443 to Redwood control-plane is denied: negotiate a customer-run control-plane proxy (approved IPs) or use an IP allowlist for package-only sync.
- If BGP is unstable during direct connect: fall back to static route entries with a monitoring script that reconciles BGP flaps and triggers a manual cutover.
- If airgapped update fails: stop the sync job, rotate the bootstrap VM, and preserve previous container images; revert to previous manifest and restart.

Operational TL;DR (quick checklist)
- Confirm non-overlapping CIDRs and peering permissions.
- Agree maintenance window and escalation contacts.
- Provision shadow infra and validate smoke tests.
- Canary cut, validate, then full cut.
- Archive terraform plan & state and note provider versions.

Common pitfalls and mitigation notes
- Overlapping internal DNS zones: create a split-horizon DNS plan and test name resolution for critical services before cut.
- MTU fragmentation on cross-connects: reduce the MTU on runtime interfaces or request jumbo frame support from colo.
- Stateful inspection boxes that rewrite ports: insist on port-preserving NAT for TLS traffic or use TLS SNI passthrough.

Operational runbook excerpt (condensed steps to execute during cut):
1) Pre-window: notify teams and set pagerduty to maintenance.
2) Run terraform plan with -target=module.shadow and save the plan file.
3) Apply shadow infra and run shadow smoke tests.
4) During canary: update LB target weights to send 5-10% of traffic to new infra. Monitor for 30 minutes.
5) If OK, increase to 50%, then 100%. If failure, roll weights back and follow rollback procedure.
6) Post-cut: remove legacy NATs and finish cleanup.

Open questions / items for follow-up:
- Create a small library of pre-signed artifacts for airgapped installs (format, signing key rotation schedule).
- Define a supported MTU matrix by provider and include it in the module docs.
- Add an automated terraform drift-checker job in the private-deployments CI that tags tenants with detected drift.

Action items (owners):
- Priya: draft the module migration helper script prototype (due 2025-02-20).
- Ethan: run canary on customer-acme testbed and report issues (due 2025-01-15).
- Ava: propose the pre-signed artifact format for airgapped installs (due 2025-01-30).

Appendix — quick terraform snippet (example usage):
# example usage (pseudocode)
# module "redwood_network" {
#   source = "github.com/redwood-inference/tf-modules//vpc?ref=v1.3.0"
#   customer_cidr = "10.100.0.0/16"
#   public_subnets = ["10.100.1.0/24","10.100.2.0/24"]
#   private_subnets = ["10.100.100.0/24","10.100.101.0/24"]
#   transit_attachment_id = null
# }

Notes on tone: keep this document pragmatic and prescriptive — the goal is to shorten decision time during on-call/onboarding and reduce back-and-forth with customer networking teams.

End of draft.
